In my life, I've eaten all I wanted, played all I wanted, and seen all I wanted. But whenever I think of that distant rainy night, that strange woman who fell into the river... I feel I still haven't seen enough. 

That night, I was chiseling jade from the mountain. Suddenly, a violent storm erupted. As I was about to find a cave to take shelter, a thunderbolt crashed, my hanging rope snapped, and I was about to fall to the cliff bottom. 
I clung tightly to the rock. Just then, a second thunderbolt struck. As I searched for a way to survive, I saw her, that strange woman, swept up by the thunderbolt, stumbling into the dark, churning water. 
She was tall and slender, not petite. But curled up like that, from a distance, she looked like an abandoned baby thrown into the water. 
I don't remember if I heard her sobs, only that she bowed her head in silence for a while, then suddenly lifted her face and shouted fiercely at the dark night sky, "Master Qu Yuan! When you threw yourself into the river, having no way to serve your country, did you also utter such a cry of utter despair?" 

Only wind and rain answered her. 

She seemed deflated, slowly sinking, letting the water surface cover her. Completely cover her. 
But just when I thought she would vanish beneath the water, suddenly, wind howled all around, phantom shadows flickered, as if countless souls traversed primordial cosmos, emitting long cries. 

"Rouge cracks into cold armor light, Jade Gate snow tempers sword-brows crimson!" The wind sounded like human speech, as if urging her to rise. 
"Say not that rosy cheeks are not iron armor, when have heroines ever yielded to men?" Her voice came from underwater, as if in response. 

A lightning bolt tore the sky. In an instant, all around became bright as day, a person stood up abruptly from the water, dragging a long dragon tail, amidst the howling wind and long cries. 
I recognized her! She was that Tang princess! 

I understand! I fully understand! Those cries that summoned her from the black waters just now must belong to Wang Zhaojun venturing beyond the frontier on a snowy night, Liu Jieyou galloping a thousand miles, Princess Wencheng knocking on Yumen's snow... belong to countless ill-fated noble daughters married far to foreign lands. 

Wind howled, the heavenly gate opened wide, torrential rain poured down. Sounds swallowed by historians' ink now all became blade-songs piercing the firmament. 
Countless princesses lifted her out of the water; and she led countless princesses, striving to climb the gate to heaven. 

Carrying the earnest hopes of a multitude, she leaped, completing this transformation into a dragon. 
And as she bowed to face the thunderstorm, they transformed into the hard scales on her back. 
Or was it really her who emerged from the water, or them? 

Together, they walked upward, toward the end of the road, returning to their origin, ascending to the sky. Amidst the torrential rain, they faced the overwhelming thunder. 

They left. 
Amidst such thunder and rain, I could no longer tell what I had seen or heard. 
What I felt, was it merely sympathy, pity, or praise for the princesses? 
No, I felt the blood flowing in my veins, the power surging in my chest. I suddenly regained immense strength, gripping the protruding rocks tightly. I would climb that high cliff. I would survive. 
I would go study, I would write poetry, I would record what I saw, so that you who read this book now may see. 
I do not know when I will die, but in the end, I did not die beneath that day's broken cliff. Nor did she.

Brother Qiang: 

I've always been a man of few words, and you used to complain about my silence. 
Now that you're locked up, I have no one to talk to, and suddenly, my heart is full of things to say. So I decided to write them all down in one go. 

Truth is, twenty years ago, I didn't run away—not out of loyalty, but because all the other kids had their own cliques and backers, while I couldn't connect with anyone. I was afraid you'd beat me up, so I just stood there, frozen. 

The day we robbed that road, I didn't run—not out of loyalty, but because I'd never heard the voice of a dying man before. It terrified me into stillness, so I just stood there, frozen. 

The day you told me to guard the money, I didn't run—definitely not out of loyalty, but because I thought of all our past and the uncertain future between us. Words failed me, so I just stood there, frozen. 

Back then, you always insisted on teaching me martial arts, wanting to take me into the jianghu. But I could never even remember the moves, so I kept making excuses. 

Later, you took the fall for me and ended up with a murder charge. We had no choice but to flee, but halfway through, all our travel money was stolen... 

At that moment, I realized—you and I, one reckless, the other dumbstruck—were like flies in this chaotic world, desperately trying to live but crashing headfirst into death. 

You always said my whole life could be summed up in one word: "frozen." Well, these past ten years, I've made sure to show you just how frozen I can be. 
This time, just pretend it's out of loyalty. 

...I've rambled so much, and it's all for nothing. 
You can't even read, anyway. When you finally see this letter, I'll just say I was reminiscing about the happy days of our childhood.
